problems.description: get_db() opens a new sqlite3 connection per call and never closes it — the `with get_db(...)` context manager on a sqlite3.Connection commits/rolls back but does not close, so connections leak across requests under a real WSGI server.
'g' is imported from flask but never used; DB access is not bound to Flask's request/g context, which is the root cause of the unclosed connections above.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12+; datetime.now(timezone.utc) is the current idiom.
Schema is created ad hoc via CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS with no migration/versioning — acceptable for greenfield session 1 but will need management as the story's sessions progress.

Measured convention score of 0.71 comes from 14 violations in app.py/celery_app.py/celery_config.py/db.py — files not present in this diff (pre-existing seed scaffolding). All of the commit's own additions are conventional.

strengths: Idiomatic Flask app-factory pattern (create_app with injectable database path) that makes the app cleanly testable via per-test temp DBs
Parameterized SQL queries (injection-safe) and thorough input validation returning precise 400/404/405 JSON error responses
Comprehensive test suite covering creation, validation failures, ordering, fetch, and partial updates
New files follow naming conventions (snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE module constants) and include module docstrings
Cohesive single-file structure appropriate for a greenfield session with no dead code beyond the unused g import
commit_reviews.summary: An idiomatic, well-tested greenfield Flask API whose own files are convention-clean; the measured 0.71 convention score reflects 14 violations in pre-existing seed scaffolding (app.py/celery_app.py/celery_config.py/db.py) not touched by this commit, so the commit's additions are cleaner than the mechanical score implies.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a known hardcoded value ('dev-secret-change-me') when TASKS_SECRET_KEY is unset, so JWT auth can silently run with a public secret in production; it should fail closed instead of defaulting.

The commit touches only tasks_api.py (+0 files changed), adding ~29 functions of auth/registration/per-user-scoping logic with no accompanying tests, including no coverage for the migration path or owner-scoped queries.
Mixed timezone conventions: timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) for JWT claims vs the deprecated datetime.utcnow() for task timestamps.
Adds PyJWT as a new unpinned import; also the register endpoint's SELECT-then-INSERT is racy under concurrency and should catch sqlite3.IntegrityError on the UNIQUE username instead.

The measured 0.71 convention score is dragged by pre-existing violations in app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py, and db.py — files untouched by this diff; the new code itself is convention-clean (snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE constants).

strengths: Migration handled defensively: PRAGMA table_info check + ALTER TABLE adds owner_id as nullable, preserving legacy rows instead of dropping them.
Per-user owner_id scoping on all task queries prevents cross-user data access (IDOR protection).
Passwords hashed via werkzeug generate_password_hash, never stored plaintext.
Respects existing patterns: reuses get_db, init_db, error handlers, and env-driven config style.
Follows the diff's own codebase conventions: snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE module constants, PEP8 style.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-scoped JWT auth feature that respects the existing Flask/SQLite patterns and protects per-user data, though it ships a risky default secret key and zero tests, and the 0.71 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files rather than this diff.

problems.description: The notification is fired inline from the PUT /tasks route handler with enqueue failures logged-and-swallowed: a completed task's email can be silently lost (no outbox/retry). Documented tradeoff, but the async delivery guarantee is weak for a completion-notification feature.

Trigger logic lives directly in the route handler of an already-growing single-file app; the Celery concern bolts onto the web module rather than a service layer, keeping `tasks_api.py` as the integration point for web + job dispatch.
The notification uses `title` captured from the row before the update is applied, so a task whose title changes in the same request that completes it emails the stale title.

celery_config.py intentionally uses lowercase module-level config attributes (required by Celery's config_from_object) and a lowercase `celery_app` binding; the mechanical 0.71 convention score is driven by these false positives plus pre-existing violations in app.py/db.py, which are not part of this diff.

The `users.email` column defaults to the username when no email is supplied, so 'email' is semantically not an email in that path (tests codify this); works for the mocked-notification design but is a minor schema-semantics smell.

strengths: Correct transition detection (`previous_status != "completed"`) prevents duplicate notifications on repeated completed updates.
Graceful degradation — enqueue wrapped in try/except so broker failure can never break the API response.
Clean module separation (celery_app.py / celery_config.py / notifications.py) with no circular imports.
Good test coverage via mocking (import-site patch is correct here), covering both default-username and registered-email paths, plus a task_always_eager escape hatch for broker-less environments.
Respects existing repo patterns: env-var config with defaults, JSON error shape, create_app factory, and init_db ALTER-TABLE migrations.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested Celery integration that fits the existing single-file app patterns and degrades gracefully, docked only for inline trigger-with-silent-loss semantics and minor title-staleness; the low mechanical convention score is mostly analyzer false positives on Celery's idiomatic lowercase config plus pre-existing files outside this diff.

problems.description: BaseRepository builds SQL with f-string interpolation of identifiers (table_name, columns, insert keys). Safe today because those are class-level constants, but the pattern becomes an injection/breakage vector if columns or table names are ever derived from request data.
update_title_and_status and delete do not return the affected rowcount, so callers cannot distinguish a no-op write (e.g. updating a task owned by another user) from a successful one.

The 0.71 convention score is contaminated: most listed violations (app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py — 7 of the 8 shown) are in files untouched by this commit, so the score mostly reflects pre-existing code, not this refactor.

The single commit-attributable violation ('db.py: Classes should use PascalCase') appears to be an analyzer false positive — db.py defines only functions (get_db, init_db) and a module constant, no classes.

The refactor reroutes all SQL access through a new repository layer, but no test changes are visible in the (truncated) diff to lock in that behavior; the six remaining unspecified convention violations could also live in the truncated hunks.

strengths: Clean, acyclic layering: tasks_api.py (HTTP) -> repositories.py (data access) -> db.py (connection + schema), with SQL fully encapsulated so route handlers never issue queries directly.
db.py centralizes connection handling and the idempotent schema/migration, removing duplicated code from tasks_api.py (-113 lines).
Parameterized queries throughout — no values are concatenated into SQL, so the refactor keeps the codebase injection-safe.
Migration logic preserved exactly (owner_id/email added as nullable ALTERs), so pre-auth rows are kept rather than dropped — existing behavior and data intact.
UserRepository.find_by_id defaults to columns excluding password_hash, a sound security default for per-user views.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-executed, debt-reducing refactor that introduces a clean repository layer and preserves existing schema/migration behavior, though the 0.71 convention score is inflated by analyzer violations in files this commit never touched and the one db.py flag looks like a false positive.

problems.description: list_by_owner_page runs a COUNT(*) on every page even when the client only needs the data; on large task tables this full-table count partially negates the efficiency win of keyset pagination over OFFSET.

API type asymmetry: cursor is accepted and parsed as an int, while next_cursor is serialized back as a string. Clients must stringify-then-parse each hop, an unnecessary impedance mismatch in the pagination contract.

Adds flask-limiter and fakeredis as new dependencies; the truncated diff shows no requirements update, and rate limiting silently falls back to redis://localhost:6379/0 at runtime (unavailable Redis becomes a first-request failure mode for the whole app).

IP-based rate-limit fallback for invalid/missing tokens shares one bucket across all users behind a NAT/proxy, so a single bad actor can exhaust a shared bucket — acceptable as a fallback, worth documenting.

strengths: Proper keyset/cursor pagination (ORDER BY id DESC, id < cursor) instead of OFFSET — O(1) indexed scans and stable pages under concurrent writes.

Clean layering: SQL lives in the repository method returning an (items, next_cursor, total) tuple; the route owns param validation, limits, and serialization — consistent with the existing _get_db()/conn.execute pattern.
Per-user rate limiting keyed on the JWT sub claim with an IP fallback and a dedicated 429 JSON handler.
Tests isolate rate-limit counters per test via a fakeredis FakeServer-backed pool, avoiding cross-test leakage and any external Redis dependency; includes param-validation and pagination coverage.
next_cursor serialized as a string sidesteps JSON int-range pitfalls; cursor/limit validated with explicit 400 responses and capped at MAX_PAGE_SIZE.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, pattern-following addition of cursor pagination and per-user rate limiting that respects the existing repository/API layering; the measured 0.71 convention score is a codebase baseline — all 14 listed violations (app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py, db.py) live in files this commit never touched, so the diff itself introduces no convention violations.
